title: Writing a Concise Weekly Status Report
titleEs: Redactar un informe de estado semanal conciso
summary: Turn a week of work into one screen a stakeholder can read on a phone: a headline (*as of Friday, on track for…*), then Done, In progress, Blocked, At risk and Next steps, with passives and nouns instead of stories, and an owner and a due date for every action.
canDo: Write a status headline with *as of* + date and *on track / at risk / off track*.
Report completed work in the Present Perfect passive and ongoing work in the present continuous passive.
Turn a chatty voice note into a structured report: mediation from informal speech to formal writing.
Say *as of* and *ahead of schedule* as single blocks, and *blocked* and *outstanding* without an extra syllable.

focus.grammar: Present Perfect passive for Done (has / have been + past participle) · present continuous passive for In progress (is / are being + past participle) · nominalisation (the inclusion of…, delay in…) · as of + date · due + date · can't … until
focus.lexis: a status report, the headline, as of, on track / at risk / off track, in progress, blocked, outstanding, due, an owner, carry over, a quick one
focus.afh: weak of: as of /əz‿əv/, ahead of schedule /əˌhed‿əv/ · clusters: blocked /blɑːkt/, risk /rɪsk/, outstanding /-tst-/ · due US /duː/ vs UK /dʒuː/

warmup: Think of a report you receive regularly: a newsletter, a team update, a bank statement. What do you read first, and what do you skip? Now imagine your stakeholder doing the same with your report.

questions.q: Compare *the four busiest pages have been migrated* (Done) and *the reporting module is being tested* (In progress). What does each verb form say about the state of the work right now? Why does neither sentence say who did it?
questions.model: *Have been migrated* is a Present Perfect passive: the work is complete, a result that exists now. *Is being tested* is a present continuous passive: the work is happening now and is not finished. Neither names the person, because a status report is about the work, not about people; the owner appears separately, next to the item, where it is actionable.
criteria: You said *have been migrated* = complete now, and *is being tested* = in progress now.
You identified both as passives (*have been / is being + past participle*).
You explained why the agent is left out: the report is about the work; the owner goes next to the item.

questions.q: Write the patterns of the two passives (*have been migrated*, *is being tested*) and of the nominalised phrase *the inclusion of the search function is at risk*. Then say the same three things as you would in a casual chat message.

signals.re: have been \+|has been \+|have been|has been|past participle
signals.label: have been + past participle

questions.model: Present Perfect passive: *have / has been + past participle*. Present continuous passive: *is / are being + past participle*. Nominalisation: *the + noun (inclusion, migration, completion) + of + noun* as the subject of *is at risk*. In chat: *we've migrated the four busiest pages*, *we're testing the reporting module*, *the search might not make it into the first release*: active verbs, pronouns and an informal *make it*.
criteria: You wrote both passive patterns correctly.
You described the nominalised pattern (*the inclusion of… is at risk*).
You gave active, personal chat versions of the same three ideas.

questions.q: Oliver's advice: headline first, Done with numbers, effort under In progress, each risk in one line with its decision date. What does this order do for Helen, who reads on her phone? What is lost if the report starts with the story of what happened in May?
questions.model: The order gives Helen the decision-relevant facts in the first line (*on track for June 20*), then the evidence (Done, with numbers), then what is moving, then what could hurt her and when she must decide. On a phone she may read only the first two lines, so they carry the status. A report that starts with May's story buries the status, reads like a justification and makes her hunt for the risk. Concise is not less information; it is information in the order the reader needs it.
criteria: You said the headline gives the status in the first line, where a phone reader will see it.
You said Done with numbers is the evidence and In progress holds the effort.
You said starting with the history buries the status and reads like a justification.

points: A status report has a fixed shape: headline (*As of + date, on track / at risk / off track for + date*), then Done, In progress, Blocked, At risk, Next steps with an owner and a due date.

Done takes results in the Present Perfect passive (or simple), with numbers: *the four busiest pages have been migrated*. In progress takes the present continuous passive or the Present Perfect Continuous: *is being tested*, *we've been testing*.
Nouns and passives keep it short and impersonal: *the inclusion of the search is at risk*, *decision due Monday*. The owner goes next to the item, not inside the sentence.
One screen: no history, no justification; each risk in one line with its decision date.
formulas: As of + date, the project is on track / at risk / off track for + date
Done: has / have been + past participle (+ number) · In progress: is / are being + past participle
Next steps: item (owner, due + date) · Blocked: can't + verb + until + clause
rule.note: Spanish reports tend to open with context and build towards the conclusion. English status reports do the opposite: conclusion first, evidence after. The reader can stop after the headline and still know where things stand.

phonetics.intro: El informe se lee en voz alta en las reuniones, y sus bloques fijos tienen formas débiles y enlaces propios: *as of* es «a-zov» y *ahead of schedule*, «a-HE-dov SKÉ-dyul». También hay grupos consonánticos que el español simplifica: *blocked* termina en /kt/, *risk* en /sk/, y *outstanding* lleva /tst/ en medio sin e de apoyo.

items.meaning: at or from that date, as the point of reference

alerts.text: *Of* es débil, /əv/: «ov», con schwa y v. No «of» con f ni con o plena.
La z de *as* se une a *of*: «a-zov», un solo bloque, y sigue sin pausa: «a-zov-FRAI-dei».
Las dos consonantes son sonoras: /z/ (zumbido) y /v/ (dientes sobre el labio). Con /s/ y /f/ suena a *as off*.

example.speaker: ryan
example.text: As of Friday, the project is on track for June 20.
example.tts: As [of](/əv/) Friday, the project is on track for June twentieth.

alerts.text: La d de *ahead* enlaza con *of*: «a-HE-dov». Tres palabras en dos golpes: «a-HE-dov SKÉ-dyul».
*Of* otra vez /əv/; *ahead* empieza con schwa y lleva el acento en HED, con h aspirada suave.
*Schedule*: US «SKÉ-dyul», UK «SHÉ-dyul», siempre sin e inicial (Lección 121). *Behind schedule* y *on schedule* funcionan igual.

example.speaker: priya
example.text: The design work is two days ahead of schedule.
example.tts: The design work is two days ahead [of](/əv/) schedule.

items.meaning: not yet done or dealt with (an outstanding item); also: excellent (an outstanding result)

alerts.text: *-tst-* en medio de la palabra: «aut-STAN», sin e entre la t y la s. Nada de «aut-es-TAN-ding».
Acento en STAN, la segunda sílaba: «aut-STÁN-ding».
/aʊ/ en *out*: el diptongo «au», breve; /æ/ en STAN: a abierta hacia la e.

example.speaker: helen
example.text: Please ensure that each outstanding item has an owner and a due date.

items.meaning: unable to continue until something outside the task is resolved

alerts.text: Tras una k sorda, -ed es /t/: «blakt», una sola sílaba. Nunca «blo-ked».
Grupo final /kt/: se oyen las dos consonantes. El hispanohablante tiende a dejar solo «blok».
US /ɑː/, abierta: «blakt». UK /ɒ/, breve y redondeada: «blokt».

example.speaker: alex
example.text: The training is blocked until legal approves the terms.

items.meaning: expected or required by that date

alerts.text: US: «duu», con d limpia. UK: «dyuu» /djuː/ (así lo dice el audio) o, en habla rápida, «dyuu» con /dʒ/ como en *jewel*. Las dos se entienden; no mezcles.
*Due on Monday*: la u enlaza con *on* sin cortar, «duu-on». *Due Friday* y *due on Friday* son las dos correctas.

l1.title: The story first
l1.text: Spanish reports build up to the conclusion. In English, the headline comes first and the context after, if at all.
l1.wrong: In May the supplier changed the format, so we had to adapt the scripts, and then… (the status at the end)
l1.right: As of Friday, the project is on track for June 20. (then the evidence)

l1.title: In process for «en proceso»
l1.text: *In process* exists but is rare and technical. The status label is *in progress*.

l1.title: Pendent for «pendiente»
l1.text: *Pending* is the adjective (*pending items*); *outstanding* is its formal equivalent. *Pendent* does not exist in this sense.

l1.title: The responsible
l1.text: Spanish *el responsable* is a noun. In English, *responsible* is only an adjective; the report word is *owner*.
l1.wrong: Search test: the responsible is Alex.
l1.right: Search test: owner Alex, due Friday.

l1.title: Is been for a passive
l1.text: Spanish *está siendo probado* maps onto *is being tested*, with *being*. *Is been* does not exist.
l1.wrong: The reporting module is been tested.
l1.right: The reporting module is being tested.

task.title: From a voice note to a status report
task.scenario: It is Friday. Alex has left you a rambling voice note with everything that happened this week. Turn it into Ryan's weekly status report for Helen: headline, Done, In progress, Blocked, At risk and Next steps, with an owner and a due date for every action. One screen.
task.brief: Mediate: from a chatty voice note to a concise status report for a stakeholder.

input.title: Alex's Friday voice note
input.speaker: alex
input.text: Hey Ryan, Friday update, sorry it's a bit all over the place. So, the indexing is done, finally; that was Tuesday. The full-scale search test: I've been running it all week, the numbers look good, but I want one more run on Monday before we decide. Training can't start; legal still hasn't approved the terms, and I've chased them twice. Oh, and Priya signed off the invoices page yesterday. Next week: I'll do the last search run on Monday, and someone needs to call legal, maybe Oliver. That's it, have a good weekend!

steps: Write the headline: *As of Friday, … on track / at risk for …*
Done: completed items in the passive, with the day or a number.
In progress: the search test. Blocked: the training, with the cause.
At risk: one line with the decision date.
Next steps: each item with an owner and a due date.

parts.tts: Portal migration, status, week twenty-one. As [of](/əv/) Friday, the project is on track for June twentieth. Done: the indexing has been completed, Tuesday; the invoices page has been signed off, Priya, Thursday. In progress: the full-scale search test is being run; results look good, with one more run on Monday. Blocked: training cannot start until legal approves the terms; chased twice. At risk: the search may not be in the first release; decision Tuesday. Next steps: final search run, Alex, due Monday; call legal, Oliver, due Monday; updated plan to Helen, Ryan, due Tuesday. Ryan
parts.label: Weekly status report (neutral, written)
notes: The headline first: *As of Friday, on track for June 20*. Nothing from the voice note's apology survives.
*Has been completed (Tuesday)*, *has been signed off (Priya, Thursday)*: Done in the passive, with the day and the person in brackets.
*Is being run; results look good*: In progress keeps Alex's *I've been running it all week* without the *I*.
*Blocked: training cannot start until legal approves the terms (chased twice)*: the complaint becomes a condition and a fact.
*Next steps* turns *someone needs to call legal, maybe Oliver* into *call legal (Oliver, due Monday)*: an owner and a date.

parts.speaker: emma
parts.text: {{As of}} 24 May, the programme {{remains on track}} for go-live on 20 June; the start of training {{is contingent on}} legal approval of the terms, which {{has been requested}} twice and {{remains outstanding}}.
parts.tts: As [of](/əv/) the twenty-fourth of May, the programme remains on track for go-live on the twentieth of June; the start of training is contingent on legal approval of the terms, which has been requested twice and remains outstanding.
parts.label: One line for the steering committee (formal)
notes: *Remains on track*: the headline in committee language.
*Is contingent on legal approval*: the blocked item as a condition, with a noun (*approval*) instead of *legal hasn't approved*.
*Has been requested twice and remains outstanding*: *I've chased them twice* in the passive, without a complaint.

selfCheck.text: Si Helen solo lee la primera línea en el móvil, ¿sabe ya si el proyecto va bien, cuál es la fecha y qué está en riesgo? Copia tu primera línea aquí y júzgala.
¿Desapareció el tono de la nota de voz (*sorry it's all over the place*, *finally*, *that's it*)? ¿Cada sección usa sustantivos y pasivas, y no *I've been running*?
¿Done lleva *has / have been + participio*, In progress *is being + participio*, y Next steps un dueño y una fecha por línea? ¿Nada de *is been tested*?
¿Escribiste *in process*, *pendent*, *the responsible* o *the 20 of June*? Debe ser *in progress*, *outstanding / pending*, *owner*, *20 June* o *June 20*.

¿Qué información de la nota de voz decidiste dejar fuera (la disculpa, *finally*, *have a good weekend*) y qué transformaste (la queja sobre legal → *Blocked: … until legal approves*)? Mediar es elegir.
